title: The Supreme Court First Gave Students Constitutional Rights, Then Gave Back Searches and Paddlings
dek: From refusing to salute the flag to searching backpacks, six rulings gradually map out the constitutional rights of public school students; the Court, while declaring that schools are not 'enclaves of totalitarianism,' also upheld corporal punishment and searches based on reasonable suspicion, narrowing the boundaries of those rights.
why: Each ruling is explained in five or six minutes, covering background and key holdings—ideal for listeners who want to grasp in one go the boundaries of speech, corporal punishment, and backpack searches in American public schools.
who: Parents, middle and high school teachers, and law students, as well as anyone wanting to understand the boundary between government power and children's rights in American public schools.
skip: Listeners familiar with the Establishment Clause can skip the second case; if you know the details of the earlier cases, jump straight to the corporal punishment and search cases after 25:40.

points.h: Flag Salute Case: Student Rights Enter the Schoolhouse
points.body: Can students really claim First Amendment rights during class? The origin of this case is actually religious: Jehovah's Witnesses families believed that saluting the flag violated the commandments against having other gods and against idolatry, so they refused to salute and pledge. In 1940, the Supreme Court ruled against them, and World War II led more school districts to require daily salutes and pledges. West Virginia expelled students who refused to recite the pledge, labeled them delinquents, and parents could be fined or even jailed. In 1943, the Court reversed 6–3, with Justice Jackson writing on Flag Day: no official can prescribe orthodoxy in politics, nationalism, religion, or other matters; students need not confess words that contradict their hearts or make empty gestures. This was the first time the Court established that students have some First Amendment rights inside school.

During the Cold War, the U.S. portrayed itself as a nation 'under God,' adding those words to the Pledge in 1954, and more public schools began reading scripture or praying before class. In 1951, the New York State Board of Regents asked religious leaders to compose a short, non-denominational prayer, leaving adoption to local districts. The district that implemented it allowed students to opt out, but parents of ten students sued anyway. In 1962, Engel v. Vitale ruled 6–1 that it was unconstitutional—the key was not coercion but that the prayer was written by the government, itself constituting an establishment of religion. Justice Black quoted Madison: it is proper to take alarm at the first experiment on our liberties; the same power that can establish Christianity to the exclusion of all other religions can establish with equal ease any particular sect of Christians. The decision sparked fierce backlash, and the plaintiff families were mocked and harassed.

In December 1965, middle and high school students in Des Moines planned to wear black armbands to class to protest U.S. involvement in Vietnam. The school announced in advance that those who refused to remove them would be suspended, yet some students—including four siblings—wore them and were suspended. In 1969, the Supreme Court ruled 7–2 for the students. The issue was not ordinary dress code but a quiet, passive expression akin to pure speech, and it did not disrupt class. Absent evidence of actual or materially substantial interference with schoolwork, school officials may not suppress student opinion. The opinion declared that public schools are not enclaves of totalitarianism, and students and teachers do not shed their constitutional rights at the schoolhouse gate. This 'substantial disruption' standard became the benchmark for campus speech. Justice Black dissented, predicting students would defy nearly all rules, which the hosts called a rather absurd slippery slope.

In 1983, Hazelwood East High School's student newspaper, The Spectrum, had two articles that troubled Principal Reynolds: one on teenage pregnancy used pseudonyms but might still identify the interviewee, and a divorce story named and criticized a student's parent. Reynolds decided to delete the entire two pages rather than just the articles, citing lack of time to edit and the need to publish before semester's end. In 1988, the Supreme Court ruled 5–3 for the school. The key distinction was between 'tolerating student speech' and 'promoting student speech': the paper was funded by the school, readers would see it as bearing the school's imprimatur, and the two pieces were indeed immature journalistically. The Court held that schools may regulate content they sponsor. This drew the first clear boundary around Tinker's rights.

points.h: Corporal Punishment Not Cruel and Unusual
points.body: Host Tracy suddenly recalled that many teachers kept wooden paddles on their desks when she was young, and research showed corporal punishment has not disappeared in the U.S. In the 1977 case Ingram v. Wright, the school's regulation paddle was less than two feet long, three to four inches wide, and half an inch thick, with one to five swats as the norm; but Ingram was hit more than 20 times in a single incident and needed medical attention. The Court did not dwell on whether this particular case was excessive; it ruled that school corporal punishment does not violate the Constitution. The Eighth Amendment protects convicted persons, and prisoners are separated from schoolchildren by the 'harsh facts of criminal conviction and incarceration'; schools are open institutions with teachers and peers as witnesses, and children go home at the end of the day. According to NEA statistics, corporal punishment remains legal in public schools in 17 states and is actually practiced in 14, with boys, Black students, and disabled students paddled at significantly higher rates.

points.h: Backpack Search Needs Only Reasonable Suspicion
points.body: In 1980, a 14-year-old New Jersey student, TLO, was reported by a teacher for smoking in the bathroom. Vice Principal Choplik searched her purse, found cigarettes and rolling papers, then continued digging and found what appeared to be marijuana and evidence of drug dealing. TLO was convicted and given one year's probation. In 1985, the Supreme Court ruled 6–3 that the search was legal. The Court acknowledged that the Fourth Amendment applies to school officials and that students have an expectation of privacy, but it must be balanced against the school's need to maintain a learning environment. Therefore, school searches need not meet the probable cause required of police; a lower threshold of reasonable suspicion suffices. The teacher's report gave the vice principal reason to suspect she had cigarettes, and the purse was the obvious place; seeing rolling papers naturally extended suspicion to marijuana, which was also reasonable.

terms.def: The standard from Tinker for disciplining student speech: there must be actual material disruption or evidence that it would substantially interfere with schoolwork.

The First Amendment provision prohibiting the government from establishing or endorsing religion; originally applied only to the federal government, later extended to states via the Fourteenth Amendment.
A lower evidentiary threshold than probable cause, applied to school officials searching student belongings.
The higher evidentiary standard required for police arrests or searches, contrasted here with the reasonable suspicion standard for in-school searches.
Punishment that inflicts physical pain, in this episode referring to paddling students on the buttocks with a wooden board.
People who can only passively receive what the state chooses to indoctrinate, without the ability to express their own views.

It can hardly be argued that either students or teachers shed their constitutional rights to freedom of speech or expression at the schoolhouse gate. This has been the unmistakable holding of this court for almost 50 years.

In our system, state-operated schools may not be enclaves of totalitarianism. School officials do not possess absolute authority over their students. Students in school as well as out of school are persons under our Constitution. They are possessed of fundamental rights which the state must respect, just as they themselves must respect their obligations to the state.
